summary: Defines a YANG data model for configuring a Layer 2 provider-provisioned VPN service. A management system takes it as input and creates device-specific configuration for the network elements.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC is a standard order form for a private link between company sites. A customer fills it in, and the provider's software turns the request into settings for each router. Because the form is standard, a customer can send the same request to any provider.

questions: yang data model for layer 2 vpn
what is the l2vpn service model
what is the difference between vpws and vpls
subtitle: A standard order form in YANG that describes a Layer 2 VPN service, so a provider's software can turn a customer's request into device settings.

tldr.problem: Providers sell Layer 2 VPN services, but a customer had no common machine-readable way to ask for one, so every provider used its own order form.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a YANG module, ietf-l2vpn-svc, with one container for VPN services and one for sites. A management system reads the request and works out the settings for each device.
tldr.outcome: It gives customers and operators one shared vocabulary for VPWS, VPLS and EVPN services over NETCONF or RESTCONF. It is a service model, so it never configures a device by itself.

today: RFC 8466 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2018, and no other RFC obsoletes or updates it. It is the IETF's Layer 2 VPN service model, and the companion document for Layer 3 VPN services is RFC 8299.

sections.title: What the Layer 2 VPN Service Model Is
sections.content:
RFC 8466 defines a YANG data model for Layer 2 VPN (L2VPN) service, called the Layer 2 VPN Service Model (L2SM). YANG is a language for describing configuration data, so the model can be read by people and parsed by software. Its elements can be used in protocols between a customer and a network operator, and as input to automated control and configuration applications.

The model covers point-to-point Virtual Private Wire Services (VPWS) and multipoint Virtual Private LAN Services (VPLS) built on pseudowires signaled with the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) or the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), as described in RFC 4761 and RFC 6624. It also covers Ethernet VPNs (EVPN) from RFC 7432, and it conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture in RFC 8342.

How the network elements are configured from this input is explicitly out of scope. The RFC also lists the Layer 2 VPN service types the model builds on: LDP- or L2TP-signaled VPWS and VPLS, BGP-signaled VPLS, IP-only LAN services, BGP MPLS-based EVPN, and EVPN VPWS.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a standard form for ordering a private link between offices. The form says what the customer wants, not how the provider's routers should be set up.

sections.title: Where the Model Sits in the Management Stack
sections.content:
The L2SM is an abstracted interface that a customer uses to request, configure and manage the parts of a Layer 2 VPN service. A typical use is as input to an orchestration layer that translates it into configuration commands for the network elements. Those commands may go out through a command line interface, or through NETCONF with device-specific YANG models.

The reference architecture in Figure 3 has a customer service requester talking L2SM to a service orchestration function, which works with a network orchestration function and a business and operations support application. The RFC says the model can be used by any component of the management system but not directly by network elements.

The RFC points to the Layer 3 VPN service model in RFC 8299 as a sibling to compare against, and to RFC 8309 and RFC 8199 for how service models relate to configuration models. It also contrasts itself with the Metro Ethernet Forum work, which covers the whole service lifecycle including billing, Service Level Agreements (SLAs), order management and lifecycle management, whereas IETF service models are typically smaller and self-contained.
sections.plainLanguage: The request goes to the provider's own software, not to a router. That software works out which devices to change and how to change them.

sections.title: The Shape of the Data Model
sections.content:
The module is named ietf-l2vpn-svc and is built so a provider can list multiple circuits of various service types for the same customer. A circuit is an end-to-end connection between two or more customer locations. The module has two main containers, vpn-services and sites, plus a vpn-profiles container that holds the identifiers the provider accepts, such as cloud and QoS profile identifiers.

Inside vpn-services, each vpn-service carries global parameters for one VPN: its vpn-id, a service type, the customer name, a topology, cloud access, frame delivery, extranet links, and the ce-vlan-preservation and ce-vlan-cos-preservation settings.

A site holds at least one network access, and several in the case of multihoming. Attachment is through a bearer, meaning the properties below Layer 2, with a Layer 2 connection on top. Which sites may exchange traffic is expressed by the VPN policy or topology. The model is modular through YANG features, such as extranet VPNs, site diversity and QoS, and it can be extended by augmentation, for example to add encapsulations beyond VXLAN. IANA has assigned the module the name ietf-l2vpn-svc and the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-l2vpn-svc.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has two main parts. One part describes the private network itself. The other part describes every office and how each one plugs in.

sections.title: Service Types, Topologies and Extranet Access
sections.content:
The vpn-svc-type parameter supports six flavors: point-to-point VPWS between two sites, point-to-point or point-to-multipoint VPWS between a set of sites, multipoint VPLS between a set of sites, multipoint VPLS with root and leaf sites that blocks leaf-to-leaf traffic, EVPN, and EVPN VPWS. Other types can be added by augmentation.

For topology the module supports any-to-any (the default), Hub-and-Spoke (Hubs can exchange traffic) and Hub-and-Spoke Disjoint (Hubs cannot). In every hub topology, Spoke sites can talk only to Hub sites. In BGP-based VPNs the management system is expected to allocate Route Targets automatically and to configure a MAC-VRF on the right provider edge devices. Each site then has a role in the topology: all sites in an any-to-any VPN MUST have the role any-to-any-role, while sites in hub topologies MUST be Hub or Spoke.

Two related containers are shortcuts. The cloud-access container controls which sites may reach a public cloud or the Internet, using permit-site or deny-site lists, and by default all sites SHOULD be permitted. The extranet-vpns container lets one VPN reach all of another. The RFC warns that if VPN A lists VPN B as an extranet, all sites in VPN B also gain access to all sites in VPN A.
sections.plainLanguage: You choose who may talk to whom. Everyone can reach everyone, or the small offices can reach only the head office, like spokes on a wheel.

sections.title: Sites, Network Accesses and Connections
sections.content:
A site represents a customer office connected to one or more VPN services, and it may have several locations. The model deals only with exterior interfaces (UNIs and NNIs); internal interfaces and the underlying topology are out of scope. A site has a site-id, devices, a management mode, locations, optional site diversity and a list of site-network-accesses.

Each site-network-access is an Ethernet logical connection to the site, and several of them are used for multihoming. The bearer says what the attachment needs below Layer 2, and the connection container sets Layer 2 parameters. The connection can be an untagged interface, a tagged interface or a LAG interface. For tagged interfaces the model defines five ways of tagging.

The model also covers CVLAN-to-service mapping, preservation of the customer VLAN ID and CoS, Layer 2 control protocol handling (each protocol can be discarded, peered or tunneled), and Ethernet service OAM using IEEE 802.1ag connectivity fault management and ITU-T Y.1731 performance monitoring. Site management comes in three common models: provider-managed, customer-managed and co-managed CE.
sections.plainLanguage: Each office can plug in with one cable or with several. The form also says how traffic is labeled and who looks after the office's own router.

sections.title: Attaching a Site to a VPN
sections.content:
A site can be part of one or more VPNs, set by its site-vpn-flavor: single, multi, nni or e2e. With single the site belongs to only one VPN. With multi it belongs to several, and all of the site's logical accesses belong to the same set of VPNs. The other two flavors mark a site that is not an ordinary customer office: nni for a boundary between two administrative domains, and e2e for an end-to-end multi-segment connection.

The attachment itself is made at the site-network-access level, in a mandatory vpn-attachment container, and there are two ways to fill it in. The first is to reference the VPN directly by vpn-id and add a site-role, which is the best fit for a single VPN attachment. The second is to reference a vpn-policy, which is needed for the more complex cases: a site that plays a Hub role in one VPN and an any-to-any role in another, or a site whose LAN segments are split between different VPNs using a filter on the LAN tag.
sections.plainLanguage: An office can join one private network or several. For each one, the form says which network it joins and whether the office is a Hub, the center of the network, or a Spoke, a branch off it.

sections.title: Choosing Where to Connect the Site
sections.content:
The management system then decides where each access connects, for example to a provider edge device or an aggregation switch. It MUST honor all customer constraints, and if a constraint is too strict it MUST NOT provision the site and MUST tell the user which constraints failed. The customer can force a particular device, name a location, ask for a particular kind of access (requested-type, strict, always-on, bearer-reference) and ask for diversity from other accesses, for example pe-diverse, pop-diverse, linecard-diverse or bearer-diverse.

On the provider edge, the management system allocates a MAC-VRF and a Route Distinguisher that MUST be unique across all MAC-VRFs on that device, or reuses an existing MAC-VRF that already fits. For availability, access-priority (higher is preferred) models primary/backup or load sharing, and redundancy-mode models single-active and active/active multihoming. The RFC gives a five-access example with priorities 100, 100, 50, 50 and 10, and notes that some scenarios cannot be expressed this way.

The RFC then works through a whole request: a VPN service for three sites, using point-to-point VPWS and a Hub-and-Spoke topology, with two Spoke sites and one Hub site. The management system allocates two Route Targets, 100:1 for Hubs and 100:2 for Spokes, picks a target PE for Spoke Site 1, and checks whether a VSI that fits is already on it. If not, it provisions one with a Route Distinguisher and the right imports and exports. The CE configuration is built the same way, ready to be loaded onto the device before it is shipped to the customer.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider has to follow the customer's wishes about where to plug in, or say which wishes it could not meet. The RFC shows a request for three sites, then the router settings the provider's software produces from it.

sections.title: Bandwidth, QoS and Shared-Resource Limits
sections.content:
The service bandwidth is configured per site network access, using the Committed Information Rate, Excess Information Rate or Peak Information Rate, with separate ingress and egress values. The parameter has four types: bw-per-access, bw-per-cos, bw-per-svc and opaque bandwidth. The svc-mtu leaf can override the MTU derived from the physical interface.

QoS is an abstraction in two parts. A qos-classification-policy is an ordered list of rules that match traffic and set a target class, and frames are marked green, yellow or red depending on whether they fit the committed rate, only the excess rate, or neither. A qos-profile chooses a standard or custom scheduling profile with direction, policing, delay, jitter and a guaranteed bandwidth percentage. By default bandwidth is guaranteed only at the access, and an end-to-end leaf requests a reservation across the transport network, though how that is done is out of scope.

For broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast (BUM) traffic, the model supports bidirectional, shared and source-based trees and two ways to map multicast groups to ports. Providers can rate-limit BUM frames at the edge. To protect shared resources, mac-loop-prevention imposes a MAC move threshold, and mac-addr-limit caps learned MAC addresses and sets the action when the limit is hit: drop the packet, flood it, or log a warning.
sections.plainLanguage: The form says how fast the link should be and which traffic should go first. It also stops one noisy office from filling the shared address book that every service on the device uses.

sections.title: Carriers' Carriers, NNIs and Inter-Provider Use
sections.content:
For Carriers' Carriers (CsC), where a customer such as an ISP builds an MPLS service over a provider's Layer 2 VPN, the VPN service sets carrierscarrier to true and the site link runs LDP or BGP as the MPLS signaling protocol. With LDP an IGP MUST also be active, and with BGP signaling BGP MUST also be the routing protocol. The requested svc-mtu then refers to the MPLS MTU.

VPNs that span autonomous systems or providers need Network-to-Network Interfaces (NNIs), modeled as a site with site-vpn-flavor-nni. In option A, a back-to-back VPLS model, a VPN connection per VPN crosses the boundary on ASBR links and can be seen as a site. In option B, VPN routes are exchanged with MP-BGP, and the RFC distinguishes cases where no modeling is needed from cases where RT-filtering policy must be maintained. Option C is modeled like option B, but the MP-BGP session is multihop between routing gateway (RGW) nodes.

For end-to-end service across domains, the RFC describes stitching connectivity segments from site to site, so that control connections run only between PEs and ASBRs and not as a full mesh. The service orchestrator is assumed to see the complete abstract topology and resource availability.
sections.plainLanguage: When a private network has to cross from one provider to another, the two providers need an agreed handover. The model has a way to order that handover.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF. NETCONF's mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH (RFC 6242), and RESTCONF's is TLS (RFC 8446). The NETCONF access control model in RFC 8341 can restrict users to a subset of the available operations and content.

The writable subtrees /l2vpn-svc/vpn-services/vpn-service and /l2vpn-svc/sites/site are sensitive because they indirectly create or modify provider edge and customer edge configuration, so unexpected changes could lead to service disruptions or network misbehavior. The same two subtrees are sensitive to read because they hold customer-confidential information such as customer name, site location and subscribed services.

When a service provider serves multiple customers, it has to ensure that each customer can view and modify only its own service information.
sections.plainLanguage: The forms hold details about customers, and changing one can change the live network. So only the right people may read or change a form, and each customer sees only its own.

viz.caption: THE FIVE WAYS TO TAG A TAGGED INTERFACE

items.label: Priority tagged
items.desc: Packets are tagged with the frame priority level between CE and PE.

items.label: 802.1Q VLAN tagged
items.desc: Packets carry one or a set of customer VLAN (CVLAN) IDs.

items.label: Q-in-Q
items.desc: Multiple CVLAN IDs plus a single SP VLAN (SVLAN) tag.

items.label: Q-in-any
items.desc: Unknown CVLANs plus a single SVLAN tag.

items.label: VXLAN
items.desc: A VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI) and a peer list.

items.title: Provider-managed CE
items.text: The provider owns the CE and only the provider can access it. The boundary is between the CE and the customer network.

items.title: Customer-managed CE
items.text: The customer owns the CE and only the customer can access it. The boundary is between the PE and the CE.

items.title: Co-managed CE
items.text: The provider owns and manages the CE but gives the customer some configuration and monitoring access.

items.label: Per access
items.desc: Rate enforcement for all service frames on a particular network access.

items.label: Per CoS
items.desc: Rate enforcement for all frames of a given CoS, which needs a cos-id.

items.label: Per service
items.desc: Rate enforcement for all frames of a particular VPN service, which needs a vpn-id.

items.label: Opaque
items.desc: Total bandwidth not tied to any cos-id, VPN service or site network access ID.
